speaker_desc: Eminent literary critic Stanley Fish, Wittgenstein expert Genia Schönbaumsfeld and post-realist philosopher Hilary Lawson scrutinise the limits of language.
subtitle: Can we find the right words for everything?

title: Poisonous Speech
description: Historic hate speech was described as a "poison" at the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg. Then, they were talking about Nazi propaganda against Jewish people. Has hate speech become a poison again? Or does today's political and social context require total free speech? Cambridge Philosopher Rae Langton examines the offence and the harm of hate speech.
subtitle: Should we ban hate speech? | Rae Langton

title: Life, Beauty and Being
description: Once beauty was about goodness and truth, now we think it means little more than models, products and outdated art. Have practical concerns and the economy of desire made aesthetics trivial and expendable? Is the goal of living beautifully a conceit of the privileged elite? In this talk, founder of Coco de Mer Sam Roddick, philosopher Bence Nanay and director of The Public Sphere Justine Kolata ask whether traditional art has higher value than Kim Kardashian's bum.
speaker_desc: Founder of Coco de Mer Sam Roddick, philosopher and film critic Bence Nanay ad director of The Public Sphere Justine Kolata ask whether paintings have higher value than Kim Kardashian's bum.
subtitle: Is beauty something we now buy?

title: Your Life in the Balance
description: Clinical errors in the UK are responsible for six times as many deaths as road accidents. Is doctors' power dangerous and should we look elsewhere, perhaps to AI technology, to regain control? In this debate, Pharmageddon author David Healy, Cambridge philosopher and author of Medical Nihilism Jacob Stegenga and Policy lead at the Medical Protection Society Pallavi Bradshaw rethink medical authority.
filename: HTLGI2018_352 Your Life in the Balance.hd.mp4
speaker_desc: In this debate, Pharmageddon author David Healy, Cambridge philosopher and author of Medical Nihilism Jacob Stegenga and Policy lead at the Medical Protection Society Pallavi Bradshaw rethink medical authority.
subtitle: Should we trust doctors less than we do?

title: The Struggle for Social Justice
description: Britain is one of the wealthiest nations in the world, so why do so many feel short-changed? Labour MP and former minister Angela Eagle sees an urgent need to protect social cohesion and makes a case for radical economic reform, to trump inequality and create a fairer society.
subtitle: Can we make rich countries fairer? | Angela Eagle

title: The Key to Creativity
description: Freedom is often seen as the vital oxygen of creativity. Yet Shakespeare worked within a framework of censorship, Don Quixote was written from prison, and Leonardo argued that art “lives on constraint and dies of freedom”. Can oppression help produce masterpieces, or do the free always write the greatest poetry? Former Poet Laureate Andrew Motion, novelist and author of A Field Guide to Reality Joanna Kavenna and hip hop artist Lowkey debate creativity and constraint.
speaker_desc: Former Poet Laureate Andrew Motion, novelist and author of A Field Guide to Reality Joanna Kavenna and hip hop artist Lowkey debate creativity and constraint.
subtitle: Do restrictions breed inventiveness?

title: Darkness, Authority and Dreams
description: 'Orders were the highest thing in my life, and I had to obey them without question.' So wrote Eichmann, organiser of the Holocaust. Hannah Arendt called that 'the banality of evil'. We know authority is dangerous yet we assume it is necessary for society to work. Should we dream of a free and flourishing world without leadership and rules? Or do we want and need leaders and authority to feed our hopes and dreams?
subtitle: Chomsky debates libertarians and future liberals

title: Documenting Death
description: Why do we record deaths and whose deaths are considered worthy of recording? Brooke Magnanti, forensic scientist and former Belle de Jour blogger investigates.
subtitle: Whose death is worth recording? | Brooke Magnanti

title: Conjuring the Universe
description: Where did the laws of nature come from? What are their origins? Eminent chemistry and science writer Peter Atkins shows how the structure of the universe emerged from very little, or even nothing at all.
subtitle: The origins of the laws of nature | Peter Atkins

title: Science, Sex and Subjectivity
description: Some feminist thinkers argue science is limited by male language and logic. Is there a radically different, feminist way of doing science? Philosophy of Science after Feminism author Janet Kourany, cognitive neuroscientist Gina Rippon and author of Inferior: How Science got Women Wrong, Angela Saini, envision a more inclusive way of doing science.
speaker_desc: Philosophy of Science after Feminism author Janet Kourany, cognitive neuroscientist Gina Rippon and author of Inferior: How Science got Women Wrong, Angela Saini, envision a more inclusive way of doing science.
subtitle: Is there a feminist way of doing science?

title: In Search of a New Reality
description: Our worlds were once human and solid, but now our lives are increasingly virtual. What place has reality in this fantasy world? Picnic Comma Lightning author Laurence Scott explores the challenges of finding meaning amidst the digital noise. Award-winning writer and BBC New Generation Thinker, Scott is the author of Picnic Comma Lightning: In Search of a New Reality.
filename: HTLGI2018_L94_IN SEARCH OF A NEW REALITY.HD.mp4
speaker_desc: Award-winning writer and BBC New Generation Thinker, Scott is the author of Picnic Comma Lightning: In Search of a New Reality.
subtitle: Meaning in the digital world | Laurence Scott

title: Trouble in Heaven
description: From Milton's Paradise Lost to bad boys and femmes fatales, we are seduced by the dark and dangerous. Could we imagine a world where the good was exciting, dramatic and fun?  Moral philosopher Christopher Hamilton, theologian and Zizek collaborator John Milbank, and Witches, Sluts and Feminists author Kristen Sollee debate darkness and light.
speaker_desc: Moral philosopher Christopher Hamilton, theologian and Zizek collaborator John Milbank, and author of Post-Human Ethics Patricia MacCormack debate darkness and light.
subtitle: Why does the dark and the dangerous attract us?

title: Against Psychiatric Diagnoses
description: Two-thirds of Brits suffer mental health issues, says the Mental Health Foundation. Lucy Johnstone argues the problem stems from a thirst for diagnosis we should seek to abandon. Medicalising mental health is a reductionist approach transforming people with problems into patients with illnesses, she argues.
speaker_desc: A consultant clinical psychologist, Johnstone is the author of Users and Abusers of Psychiatry and A Straight Talking Introduction of Psychiatric Drugs.
subtitle: These treatments are dangerous | Lucy Johnstone

title: Medicine's Mistakes
description: From flawed evidence to the frequency of failed medical interventions, is confidence in medicine misplaced? Cambridge philosopher Jacob Stegenga makes the case. A philosopher of science and medicine at the University of Cambridge, Stegenga is the author of Medical Nihilism published by the OUP.
subtitle: Should we distrust medicine? | Jacob Stegenga

title: Stranger Than We Think
description: We dismiss the supernatural as the stuff of fairytale and fantasy. Yet Wittgenstein argued that science is mistaken in making it look as if everything can be said. Is our continuing interest in the supernatural and paranormal a sign of an underlying truth about the limits of human understanding? Novelist and author of Hot Milk Deborah Levy, philosopher Julian Baggini and BBC New Generation Thinker and author of Picnic Comma Lighting Laurence Scott unravel the unknown.
speaker_desc: Novelist and author of Hot Milk Deborah Levy, philosopher Julian Baggini and BBC New Generation Thinker and author of Picnic Comma Lighting Laurence Scott unravel the unknown.
subtitle: Do beliefs in the supernatural reflect our limits?

title: Decolonising Britain
description: Why is the post-colonial identity only being created in the colonies, and not at the centre of the former empires, too? Is the Rhodes Must Fall movement just about pink-haired students fighting against a statue? Journalist and SOAS academic Myriam Francois argues that Britain needs a radical overhaul of its traditions and institutions. Francois covers France and the Middle East for the New Statesman and as a BBC1 presenter.
subtitle: Creating post-colonial identity | Myriam Francois

title: Socialist Dreams
description: From Stalin's gulags to weak growth in planned economies to the fall of the Berlin Wall, socialism has a chequered history. Is it a mistake to imagine that equality can be engineered through socialist planning? Should we be sceptical of those wrapped in fine ideals or is there a form of socialism that can deliver on the dream?
speaker_desc: Equal is Unfair author Yaron Brook, economist and The Making of Global Capitalism author Leo Panitch, vice chair of the Conservative party for Candidates Kemi Badenoch and philosopher and activist Judith Balso debate the perils and promise of socialism.
subtitle: Is there a form of socialism that could work?

title: How to See Things Clearly
description: Named among the Financial Times' best books of the decade, author of Willful Blindness Margaret Heffernan outlines how and why institutions and individuals need to open their eyes to information they do not want to know.
subtitle: Overcoming Willful Blindness | Margaret Heffernan

title: Overcoming death
description: From gene therapy to cryonic frozen corpses, many hope to find a way to live forever. Some scientists are starting to think death might be reversible. But Heidegger famously thought life's transience gave it meaning. Does our fear of death prevent us from living fully? Philosopher and author of Post-human Ethics Patricia MacCormack, Oxford transhumanist Anders Sandberg and author Janne Teller debate cryonics, death and where life gets its meaning.
speaker_desc: Philosopher and author of Post-human Ethics Patricia MacCormack, Oxford transhumanist Anders Sandberg and author Janne Teller debate cryonics, death and where life gets its meaning.
subtitle: Does fearing death prevent us from fully living?

title: Tribal roots and tribal conflict
description: Can we justify tribal allegiances, from the family to the nation, or are they a source of conflict, sexism, racism, nationalism, xenophobia? Post-colonial theorist Homi Bhabha, activist Yassmin Abdel-Magied, political theorist and author of Strangers in Our Midst David Miller and former Conservative politician Stephen Dorrell debate tribal division.
speaker_desc: Post-colonial theorist Homi Bhabha, activist Yassmin Abdel-Magied, political theorist and author of Strangers in Our Midst David Miller and former Conservative politician Stephen Dorrell debate tribal division.
subtitle: Can we justify our tribal allegiances?

title: Dream Hoarders
description: How might the middle class be hoarding opportunity like the upper class hoard wealth? Economist and author of Dream Hoarders Richard Reeves explores inequality, dreams and blame.
subtitle: Are we to blame for inequality? | Richard Reeves

title: Limits of Thought: John McWhorter and Stanley Fish
description: In this combative one-on-one debate, eminent literary theorist Stanley Fish debates linguist and author of The Language Hoax John McWhorter on the limits of language and thought.
speaker_desc: Stanley Fish is a literary critic and legal scholar, regularly contributing to The New York Times and is the author of multiple books, including Winning Arguments . John McWhorter is Associate Professor of English and Comparative Literature at Columbia University, specialising in linguistics and music history.
subtitle: Can we think outside of language?

title: Vanity, Victory and Vice
description: Is self-obsession an effective life strategy? Could narcissism, as Nietzsche suggests, be an important part of being true to ourselves? Or does true genius require self-doubt?
speaker_desc: Romanticist Shahidha Bari, psychologist Steven Taylor, comedian Helen Lederer and art historian Sussan Babaie debate the self and the selfie.
subtitle: Is narcissism an effective life strategy?

title: Truth and poetry
description: Where does poetry get its power? How can it reveal truths where reason and prose might fail? Hear former Poet Laureate Andrew Motion perform and explore the way of ideas.
subtitle: Andrew Motion | Where does poetry gets its power?

title: Sex robots and love machines
description: Virtual Reality pornography is already with us, along with predictions that sex robots will be commonplace by 2025. Should we endorse a future where sexual desires can be satisfied by machines? Computer scientist  and author of Turned On: Science, Sex and Robots, scientist and author of Sex, Lies and Statistics Brooke Magnanti (also known by her pen name Belle de Jour) and robot ethicist Alan Winfield seek ways forward.

title: Rethinking Science and Spirituality
description: Science has long been seen as opposing spirituality. Might this be mistaken? Biologist and author of The Science Delusion Rupert Sheldrake makes the case for the science of faith. Biologist whose research into parapsychology and evolution led to the theory of morphic resonance. He authored The Science Delusion.
subtitle: Rupert Sheldrake | They complement each other

title: Being Human and Being Good
description: We think that being moral is an essential part of being human. Yet what we see as good differs from person to person and from culture to culture. Is morality just a story we tell ourselves rather than a set of rules we must follow? Is there much more to life than being good, or are we right to to value virtue so highly?
speaker_desc: Psychologist Simone Schnall, Cambridge philosopher Rae Langton and anthropologist and author of Becoming Sinners Joel Robbins rethink meaning, morality and what it is to be human.
subtitle: Is morality relative?

title: Making Sense of Reality
description: We think we see the world the way it is. But how we think changes what we see, and more radically every organism sees the world in its own unique way. Is this because perception does not simply reflect reality but plays a part in creating it? If so, what is reality, and what are the limits on how it can be perceived?
subtitle: Do we see what they tell us to see?

title: Thinking Across the World
description: How have ideas across the world shaped the places from which they emerged? Author of How The World Thinks Julian Baggini explores global thinking and its varied influence on our cultures, our ideals and how we see ourselves.
subtitle: Julian Baggini | Non-western philosophy traditions

title: Demons of Democracy
description: 'Democracy is the worst form of government, except for all others,' said Winston Churchill. But votes can polarise nations and empower demagogues – and even Hitler rose to power through democratic means. Could alternatives from create a better society? Green Party politician Natalie Bennett, Opposing the Rule of Law author Nic Cheeseman, and Independent columnist Yasmin Alibhai-Brown seek alternatives to the system.
speaker_desc: Green Party politician Natalie Bennett, Opposing the Rule of Law author Nic Cheeseman, and Independent columnist Yasmin Alibhai-Brown seek alternatives to the system.
subtitle: Are there any better alternatives to democracy?

title: The Stuff of the Universe
description: Despite helping scientific progress, materialism does not account for experience or thought, and the particles of contemporary physics have disappeared. Should we see the world as being at least partly immaterial, or can material stuff alone explain the universe? CERN physicist John Ellis, Consciousness author Susan Blackmore and Closure theorist Hilary Lawson test our materialist worldview.
speaker_desc: CERN physicist John Ellis, Consciousness author Susan Blackmore and Closure theorist Hilary Lawson test our materialist worldview.
subtitle: Is materialism wrong?

title: Out of Control
description: Global oligopolies, from Amazon and Apple to Facebook and Google, manipulate public behaviour on an unprecedented scale. Can governments fight back and if so, how? Oxford Internet Institute researcher and former Google employee James Williams, Times columnist David Aaronovitch, and entrepreneur and author of Willful Blindness Margaret Heffernan scrutinise the power the tech giants have over us.
speaker_desc: Oxford Internet Institute researcher and former Google employee James Williams, Times columnist David Aaronovitch, and entrepreneur and author of Willful Blindness Margaret Heffernan scrutinise the power the tech giants have over us.
subtitle: How dangerous are the tech giants?

title: Morality and Mindfulness
description: Does meditation make us more ethical? From mobile apps to luxury retreats, mindfulness is all the rage. Does our embrace of this practice raise important ethical questions? Buddhist and broadcaster Vishvapani Blomfield investigates a thoroughly modern phenomenon.
subtitle: Vishvapani Blomfield | Can meditation fix ethics?

title: Killer Stories
description: Story telling is dangerously seductive, from rewards in the afterlife – think suicide bombers – to fear-mongering conspiracy theories. Why do stories bewitch us? Are narratives misleading, or survival tools more vital now than ever? Literary critic and author of Winning Arguments Stanley Fish, philosopher and sociologist Renata Salecl and director of A Pervert's Guide to Cinema Sophie Fiennes explore how stories win us over.
speaker_desc: Literary critic and author of Winning Arguments Stanley Fish, philosopher and sociologist Renata Salecl and director of A Pervert's Guide to Cinema Sophie Fiennes explore how stories win us over.
subtitle: Why do we fall for narratives?

title: Stories of Life and Law
description: Barristers in our courts must weave complex stories around the black and white of law. Can our legal system ever keep its promise of justice? Criminal barrister and author of ‘In Your Defence’ Sarah Langford tells her story of representing the mad, the bad and the vulnerable.
subtitle: When a lawyer represents those in the wrong

title: The Dark Universe
description: According to current theories, Dark Energy and Dark Matter make up 95% of all the stuff in the universe. Yet we still have no direct evidence for them. Is something radically wrong? Theoretical physicist at the Frankfurt Institute for Advanced Studies Sabine Hossenfelder, winner of the Spinoza Prize Erik Verlinde, and European Research Council Fellow Catherine Heymans question the latest theories on dark matter.
speaker_desc: Theoretical physicist at the Frankfurt Institute for Advanced Studies Sabine Hossenfelder, winner of the Spinoza Prize Erik Verlinde, and European Research Council Fellow Catherine Heymans question the latest theories on dark matter.
subtitle: Are theories of dark matter and dark energy true?

title: The Fractured Mind
description: Is it better for us to resist temptations or avoid them altogether? Philosopher of perception and action Bence Nanay argues that our ability to say no is connected with the fragmentation of our minds.
subtitle: Bence Nanay | Should we avoid temptations?

title: The Good, the Bad and the Artist
description: In the wake of the Weinstein scandal, many called for a boycott of the films of Roman Polanski and Woody Allen. Can and should we separate the artist from the art? Legendary literary critic Stanley Fish, activist and artist Emma Sulkowicz, known for their Mattress Performance, novelist Nell Stevens and Cambridge University Life Fellow John Harvey explore the old and new tensions between morality and art.
speaker_desc: Legendary literary critic Stanley Fish, activist and artist Emma Sulkowicz, known for their Mattress Performance, author of Mrs Gaskell & Me Nell Stevens, and author of The Poetics of Sight and Cambridge University Life Fellow John Harvey explore the old and new tensions between morality and art.
subtitle: Should we separate the artist from the art?

title: Authority, Liberty and Wealth
description: Is the Chinese model for development more efficient for economic development? Or is greater democracy still the cure rather than the disease? Yu Jie, the Head of China Foresight at LSE IDEAS, Jeremy Waldron, Professor of Legal and Political philosophy at New York University, and author of Bourgeois Values Deirdre McCloskey debate the link between prosperity, democratic and central government rule.
speaker_desc: Yu Jie, the Head of China Foresight at LSE IDEAS, Jeremy Waldron, Professor of Legal and Political philosophy at New York University, and author of Bourgeois Values Deirdre McCloskey debate the link between prosperity, democratic and central government rule.
subtitle: Is 'The China Model' better than democracy?

title: How to Make the World Better
description: Want to change the world for the better? Hear how to turn your beliefs into actions with Peter Tatchell, the LGBTQ activist who tried to arrest Mugabe, got arrested during the World Cup in Russia and is far from finished trying to change the world.
subtitle: Peter Tatchell on activism that works

title: Is Reality an Illusion?
description: Is a world independent of the observer an illusion? Or did Heisenberg and quantum physics get it wrong? Nobel prize winning physicist Gerard 't Hooft, Chiara Marletto – Oxford University pioneer of the new fundamental theory of physics Constructor Theory, and Oxford philosopher of science Chris Timpson reassess the idea of objective physical reality.
speaker_desc: Nobel Prize-winning physicist Gerard 't Hooft, Constructor Theory pioneer and Oxford physicist Chiara Marletto, and Oxford philosopher of science Chris Timpson reassess the idea of an objective physical reality.
subtitle: Quantum physics, objective and subjective reality

title: Rethinking Inequality
description: The Equal Pay Act is almost 50 years old. So why does it still pay to be a man? Leader of the Women's Equality Party Sophue Walker outlines a new feminist approach to economics.
subtitle: Sophie Walker | On feminist economics

title: The Case Against Marriage
description: We're often told that being single is bad for our wellbeing, happiness and health. But might it actually be better to remain single for some? Social psychologist and author Bella DePaulo shatters the stereotypes of singledom and makes the case against marriage and coupling up.
subtitle: Bella DePaulo | The single life can be fulfilling

title: I am not a brain
description: Many believe the mystery of consciousness will be solved once we understand the brain. Philosopher and author of 'I Am Not A Brain' Markus Gabriel challenges scientific complacency and argues for a different view of the self, the mind and human freedom.
subtitle: Why the mind is more than matter

title: A Tale of Love and Hate
description: We think love an indisputable force for good. Yet from Jihadi John to Anders Breivik, extremists often cite love of creed or country to justify atrocity. Might love of a person or group also be the origin of prejudice and hatred towards others? Are love and hatred forever entwined as Freud suggested? Or can we imagine a society built on love and free from tribalism? Former Archbishop of Canterbury Rowan Williams, psychoanalist and philosopher Renata Salecl and Oxford philosopher and author of Autobiophilosophy Robert Rowland-Smith explore the intricacies of  two of the deepest human emotions.
speaker_desc: Former Archbishop of Canterbury Rowan Williams, psychoanalist and philosopher Renata Salecl and Oxford philosopher and author of Autobiophilosophy Robert Rowland-Smith explore the intricacies of two of the deepest human emotions.
subtitle: Are love and hate inextricably linked?

title: Big Bang creation myths
description: The universe began with the Big Bang. Or so our children are taught. The Big Bang theory won out over the Steady State alternative 50 years ago because we discovered the universe was expanding. But now we know we were wrong, and it is in fact accelerating away from us. Might the whole Big Bang theory be mistaken? How could there be a beginning anyway? Is the theory of the universe’s origin just another creation myth, or is it still the best account we’ve got? And where do the sequential universe theory and the multiverse theory reside within that?
speaker_desc: Oxford mathematical physicist and philosopher of science Roger Penrose, Caltech physicist Sean Carroll and cosmologist Laura Mersini-Houghton scrutinise the beginning of the universe.
subtitle: Is the Big Bang theory mistaken?

title: The Darkest Dictator: Orwell vs Huxley
description: Orwell vs Huxley: George Orwell’s 1984 offered a terrifying vision of totalitarian rule. But in a letter to Orwell, Huxley claimed the future of society wasn’t “flogging people into obedience” but making them “love their servitude”. Are we most at risk of dictatorship when we are most content? Or are the real dangers always force and oppression?
speaker_desc: Award-winning writer and former UN and EU macroeconomist Janne Teller, author of George Orwell: English Rebel Robert Colls and author of Democracy Squared Jon Barnes weigh up the perils of political systems.
subtitle: Should we fear complacency as much as oppression?

title: The Left, the Right and the Righteous
description: The left has traditionally seen itself as progressive, with history and morality on its side. But is history on anyone's side? And as for morality, don't all politicians think they're in the right? Should the left then give up its claim to the moral high ground and argue for policies on pragmatic grounds alone? Or would this be to undermine its very core and meaning?
speaker_desc: Leader of the Women's Equality Party Sophie Walker, outspoken Mail on Sunday columnist Peter Hitchens, and Labour MP and former vicar Chris Bryant debate the left, the right and the wrong.
subtitle: Does the left hold the higher moral ground?

title: The Evolution of Suicide
description: What are the evolutionary roots of suicide? Evolutionary psychologist Nicholas Humphrey explores the science behind a dark human impulse.
speaker_desc: A note on suicide: In the UK, Samaritans can be contacted on 116 123 or email jo@samaritans.org . In the US, the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline is 1-800-273-8255 . In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international suicide helplines can be found at www.befrienders.org .
subtitle: Nicholas Humphrey | Self-killing's genetic history

title: Minds, Machines and Magic
description: We think creativity is a uniquely mysterious force. But with Google's Magenta producing musical symphonies, some fear AI threatens to make the imagination redundant. Is human creativity no more than mechanics? Will AI transform and enrich the human experience? Or is there something strange about creative thought that separates humans and machines?
speaker_desc: University of Sussex Professor of Cognitive Science Margaret Boden, cosmologist and author of How Can Physics Underlie the Mind George Ellis and best-selling sci-fi author Warren Ellis explore the possibilities and limitations of the human mind and machines.
subtitle: Is human creativity no more than mechanics?

title: The Poetry of the Universe
description: How do life and meaning emerge from physical stuff? Is quantum physics just another story we tell ourselves to explain human experience? Pioneering physicist and humanist Sean Carroll argues that the universe is made of stories, not atoms.
subtitle: Sean Carroll | We are made of stories, not atoms

title: Lost in Space
description: From Star Wars to Avatar, Hollywood's obsession with galactic space travel assumes that one day humans will colonise interstellar space. Yet the sheer size of space seems to make this theoretically impossible. At maximum speeds it would take a century to reach the nearest habitable planets, let alone return. Will human ingenuity enable us to crack the impossible? Or should we accept that we are forever alone in the universe and treasure our earth more? CERN physicist and King's College Theoretical Physics Professor John Ellis, Oxford University Fellow at the Future of Humanity Institute Anders Sandberg and General Manager at the National Space Academy Kierann Shah explore the possibilities of space travel.
speaker_desc: CERN physicist and King's College Theoretical Physics Professor John Ellis, Oxford University Fellow at the Future of Humanity Institute Anders Sandberg and General Manager at the National Space Academy Kierann Shah explore the possibilities of space travel.
subtitle: Is space travel a Hollywood fantasy?

title: The scars of history
description: "Borders are the scars of history" claimed the founders of the European Union. But in 2017 the migration crisis led France, Germany and others to reimpose checks on their previously open boundaries. Did the dream of a borderless world miss something essential about community? Author of Cosmopolitanism Kwame Anthony Appiah, British Conservative MP Kwasi Kwarteng and Kurdish independence movement activist Elif Sarican investigate nationalism.
speaker_desc: Author of Cosmopolitanism Kwame Anthony Appiah, British Conservative MP Kwasi Kwarteng and Kurdish independence movement activist Elif Sarican investigate nationalism. Prospect Magazine's Managing Editor Sameer Rahid hosts.
subtitle: Are borders the source of prejudice and conflict?

title: Truth and the Universe
description: If once we made sense of the world with the idea of God, now most of us believe in the scientific story of the unfolding universe and evolution. Yet scientists increasingly see their theories as useful models rather than an ultimate account. Might science be just another human description limited by language, culture and our particular circumstances? Or are we right to assume science has uncovered the eternal truths of the universe?
speaker_desc: Author of A Field Guide to Reality Joanna Kavenna, renowned Oxford chemist Peter Atkins and Cambridge philosopher of science Tim Lewens scrutinise the limits of science.
subtitle: What are the limits of science?

title: Mysteries of the Multiverse
description: Can we ever observe universes beyond our own? Astrophysicist Catherine Heymens reveals the latest innovations that might help map out the multiverse.
subtitle: Catherine Heymans | Observing other universes now

title: The Mind and the World
description: Is the mind just a part of the world? Or is the world all in the mind? Neither, argues physician, philosopher and poet Raymond Tallis as he puts forward his take on how we make sense of experience. 'One of Britain's greatest intellectual all-rounders' Guardian
subtitle: Raymond Tallis | The issue with neuromania

title: Innocence and Punishment
description: "Innocent until proven guilty" is a core principle of our democracy. Yet from the BBC's coverage of the Cliff Richard raid to the social media storms around #metoo, it seems we are increasingly happy to destroy reputations and careers before the proof is in. Can trial by media be more effective than the legal system? Is the individual less important than the social good? Or is the presumption of innocence an essential cornerstone of a free society?
speaker_desc: Performance artist and anti-rape activist Emma Sulkowicz, TV presenter David Aaronovitch, and barrister and author Sarah Langford discuss the metoo media trials.
subtitle: Can trial by media fix a flawed judiciary?

title: Why Things Get Better
description:
Steven Pinker's global bestseller Enlightenment Now was hailed by Bill Gates as "the most inspiring book I've ever read" but dismissed by philosopher John Gray as "unenlightened and embarrassing".

Channel 4 news presenter and LBC host Matt Frei engages Pinker in a frank discussion of his work and its critics, while Pinker lays out the case that now really is the best time to be alive.
subtitle: Steven Pinker on the world's bright future.

title: A New Sort of Socialism | Leo Panitch
description: What is the 21st century left? The unexpected rise of Bernie Sanders and Jeremy Corbyn seemed to hail the resurgence of the left. What's next for this most contested of ideologies? Distinguished Research Professor of Political Science and Canada Research Chair in Comparative Political Economy at York University Leo Panitch maps a path for socialism's future.
subtitle: Leo Panitch | What is the 21st century left?

title: Quantum Effects in Gravity
description: Despite decades of speculations, no viable proposal to detect quantum effects in gravity has yet been proposed. But the new Constructor theory has emerged to propose a new class of experiments. Oxford's physicist Chiara Marletto makes the case.
subtitle: Chiara Marletto | A new theory in physics

title: Presidents, Policies and Power
description: There are many who see Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as a threat to world peace. But they are in power because some of us also believe that strong leaders are good for us. Is the mistake to imagine that leaders can solve our problems? Can we imagine a politics where we did not vote for individuals but only for policies? Or do we need leaders however flawed they might be? Author of Democracy Squared Jon Barnes, The Guardian's China correspondent and foreign leader writer Tania Branigan, Labour MP Jess Phillips and professor of history and politics of modern China at Oxford University Rana Mitter explore our complicated relations with strong leading men and women. Isabel Hilton hosts.
speaker_desc: Author of Democracy Squared Jon Barnes, The Guardian's China correspondent and foreign leader writer Tania Branigan, Labour MP Jess Phillips and professor of history and politics of modern China at Oxford University Rana Mitter explore our complicated relations with strong leading men and women. Isabel Hilton hosts.
subtitle: Do we need strong leaders for good policies?

title: Why Philosophy Won't Go Away
description: Has science killed philosophy as Hawking famously claimed? What would Plato make of the debates between psychoanalysts and tiger mums, atheists and the religious, or search engines like Google? Author of ‘Plato at the Googleplex’ Rebecca Goldstein returns to philosophy's roots and makes her case for why humanity can't thrive without it.
subtitle: Rebecca Goldstein | Plato in the Age of Google

title: Democracy in Crisis
description: We all believe in democracy – even Vladimir Putin and Bashar al-Assad claim to abide by majority voting. But in an age when the public can be so easily manipulated and misled, can we be sure that the people know best? Should we constrain democracy and hand ever more authority to experts? Or do we, like Brexit and Donald Trump supporters hoped, need more direct democracy, and for our representatives to be messengers of the people? Research Director of the Demos Centre for the Analysis of Social Media and author of Death of the Gods: The New Global Power Grab Carl Miller, Former Shadow Secretary of State for Business, Innovation and Skills Angela Eagle, political theorist and author of Red Tory: How Left and Right Have Broken Britain and How We Can Fix It Phillip Blond question the tension between expertise and popular vote.
speaker_desc: Research Director of the Demos Centre for the Analysis of Social Media and author of Death of the Gods: The New Global Power Grab Carl Miller, Former Shadow Secretary of State for Business, Innovation and Skills Angela Eagle, political theorist and author of Red Tory: How Left and Right Have Broken Britain and How We Can Fix It Phillip Blond question the tension between expertise and popular vote.
subtitle: Should we give more or less power to experts?

title: Truth and beauty
description: The Nobel Prize winning physicist and anti-matter proponent Paul Dirac wrote "It's more important to have beauty in one's equations than to have them fit experiment". Yet many argue that simple laws, from general relativity to string theory, can never encapsulate our multi-layered, complicated reality. Can the complexity of existence ever be fully understood? Or is simplicity the key to being able to explain life and the universe? Wolf Prize winning physicist famous for his work on general relativity Sir Roger Penrose, Frankfurt Institute physicist Sabine Hossenfelder and author of Why The World Does Not Exist Markus Gabriel scrutinise the simple and the beautiful in science and philosophy.
speaker_desc: Wolf Prize-winning physicist Sir Roger Penrose, Frankfurt Institute physicist Sabine Hossenfelder and author of Why The World Does Not Exist Markus Gabriel scrutinise the simple and the beautiful in science and philosophy.
subtitle: Do beautiful theories really explain the world?

title: The Laws of the Universe
description: Since Newton, we have assumed that the universe is governed by unchanging laws, and Stephen Hawking once even argued that we were close to uncovering them in their entirety. But are these laws really eternal features of the universe? If so, how do they emerge and how do they act? Or are they merely human ways of codifying the world, which remains somehow unknowable and inexplicable?
speaker_desc: Nobel Prize-winning physicist Gerard 't Hooft joins Helen Beebee, Manchester's Samuel Hall Professor of Philosophy and President of the Aristotelian Society, and UNC-Chapel Hill cosmologist and professor of physics Laura Mersini-Houghton explore the laws of nature.
subtitle: Are the laws of nature just human constructs?

title: The Arc of Life: Tariq Ali
description: He was friends with Malcolm X and Yoko Ono, debated the Vietnam War with Kissinger, and allegedly inspired songs by the Rolling Stones and John Lennon. This is your chance to hear Tariq Ali's account of life, conviction and radical ideas.
subtitle: The activist and writer on his life and ideas

title: The secrets of the world
description: We seem to make constant progress in understanding the world and yet the biggest questions from the nature of consciousness to the nature of matter remain unsolved. Are we mistaken to assume that such questions can be answered? Might the solutions be beyond us or is the world itself beyond description? Or round the corner are the world's secrets to be found? New York Institute of Philosophy professor Paul Boghossian, biologist and author of The Science Delusion Rupert Sheldrake, Royal Holloway Senior Philosophy Lecturer Rebecca Roache and author of Closure Hilary Lawson explore the line between the known and the unknown.
speaker_desc: NYU Silver Professor of Philosophy Paul Boghossian, biologist and author of The Science Delusion Rupert Sheldrake, Royal Holloway philosopher Rebecca Roache and author of Closure Hilary Lawson explore the line between the known and the unknown.
subtitle: Can we have a complete description of reality?

title: The Science of Psychedelics
description: Is Britain's attitude to drugs ranging from LSD and MDMA to marijuana harming mental health patients? Imperial College psychiatrist and former government drugs adviser David Nutt argues for an evidence based revolution in drugs policy, and outlines how they can help treat illnesses such as depression or PTSD.
subtitle: David Nutt | Can drugs transform mental health?

title: The edge of reality
description: From the bottom of a black hole to the beginning of time, our core theories break down at the universe's extremes. Most assume this collapse of the laws of Newtonian physics in quantum physics identifies cracks in the very fabric of reality. But might it be that our theories are misguided? Are we mistaking mathematical metaphors for reality or is there something contradictory about the universe itself? Templeton Prize winning world leading physicist George Ellis, Durham professor of philosophy and author of How The Las of Physics Lie Nancy Cartwright and post-post-modern philosopher Hilary Lawson investigate the gap between mathematics and reality.
speaker_desc: Templeton Prize-winning physicist George Ellis, Durham professor of philosophy and author of How The Laws of Physics Lie Nancy Cartwright and post-postmodern philosopher Hilary Lawson investigate the gap between mathematics and reality.
subtitle: Where mathematical metaphors meet reality

title: The Future of Sex Robots and Relationships
description: Technology has been blamed for increased loneliness and the breakdown of relationships. Might it instead provide a solution? What would a sex robot experience feel like? Could sex robots change humanity? Computer scientist Kate Devlin puts forward a radical vision for the future.
subtitle: Kate Devlin | Could robots fix our erotic lives?

title: The Fires of Progress
description: Most think that social progress should be driven by ideas and persuasion not force. Yet from the French and Russian Revolutions to the Suffragettes, violent action has been instrumental to creating a better world. Are struggle and conflict the forces of progress rather than reason? Is violence ever justified as a political strategy? Or should we always venerate Gandhi over Guevara? Author of the Enlightenment Now and social psychologist Steven Pinker, political activist and author of The Dilemmas of Lenin Tariq Ali and activist of the Kurdish women's movement Elif Sarican investigate progress. Oxford Professor of History Rana Mitter hosts.
speaker_desc: Author of Enlightenment Now and Harvard cognitive psychologist Steven Pinker, political activist and author of The Clash of Fundamentalisms Tariq Ali and activist of the Kurdish women's movement Elif Sarican investigate progress. Oxford Professor of History Rana Mitter hosts.
subtitle: Steven Pinker debates violence, ideas and progress

title: Monarchy, Caste and Inheritance
description: From the Royal family to the Untouchables of the Indian caste system, we know the accident of birth has a radical and unfair impact on our lives. Do we accept this because we think the family essential to society? Could we imagine a world where family ties and inheritance were broken in favour of a more equal world? Is a high inheritance tax enough to fix that? Or would this undermine the very thing that gives our life meaning?
subtitle: Must an equal world abolish all family privilege?

title: How Science Tells Us Who We Are
description: How do environment and biology interplay to shape our identity? Do genetics explain our behaviour better than our formative experiences do? Tackling nature and nurture, Templeton Prize-winning cosmologist George Ellis, currently a distinguished professor of complex systems at the University of Cape Town in South Africa, reveals the complex mechanisms that make us who we are.
subtitle: George Ellis | Nature vs nurture

title: Capitalism, Poverty and Progress
description: Might unrestricted capitalism work better for the poor than any alternative? Is the American Dream closer to reality than socialist ideals? Author of Bourgeois Equality Deirdre McCloskey makes the case that from 1840s Manchester to modern India the market thrives when free.
subtitle: Deirdre McCloskey | Free markets empower the poor

title: Minds, Madness, Medicine
description: Deaths from heart disease have fallen by almost two thirds since the 1960s.Yet outcomes for those with mental illness, from depression and anxiety to schizophrenia and bipolar disorders, have not improved for decades. Is this because we have the wrong diagnoses? Might neuroscience provide more precise descriptions and therefore more effective treatment? Or is mental health too complex for us to understand it in mere biological terms?

title: Dreams of Equality
description: Are Beyonce and Simone de Beauvoir feminists really on the same side? How much do the second, third and fourth wave feminists share? Do successful women who make it to the top risk reinforcing a man's world while doing little about gender inequality? Or as feminism eradicates current forms of gender inequality are new forms of social division inevitably created? TV Presenter and academic Myriam Francois, former editor of the Erotic Review Rowan Pelling and performance artist known as "The Mattress Girl" Emma Sulkowicz explore the complexities of feminism, gender and inequality today.
speaker_desc: TV Presenter and academic Myriam Francois, former editor of the Erotic Review Rowan Pelling and performance artist Emma Sulkowicz explore the complexities of feminism, gender and inequality today.
subtitle: What does mainstream feminism promise?

title: The new Enlightenment
description: 'Dare to know' was the radical rallying cry of the Enlightenment. Since then philosophers from Nietzsche to Derrida have argued there are limits to knowledge so profound that truth is an impossible goal. Is the Enlightenment dream over? Or can we forge a New Enlightenment that abandons ultimate truth but provides us with direction and is equally radical and exciting as the original?
speaker_desc: Editor of The Philosophers' Magazine Julian Baggini, Dartmouth University philosophy professor Amie Thomasson and post-postmodern philosopher Hilary Lawson investigate the Enlightenment.
subtitle: Can we reclaim objectivity after relativism?

title: Is Big Data A Big Mistake?
description: Big Data is now a $300 billion industry and our personal data sold to the highest bidder. Yet data failed to predict the US election and some experts claim it leads to racist algorithms. Does data inevitably generate prejudice and error? Do we need to limit the use of data and find new narratives to make sense of the world? Or does data give us greater understanding than theory ever could?
speaker_desc: Philosopher James Ladyman, Oxford Fellow at the Future of Humanity Institute Anders Sandberg, Warwick University sociology professor Noortje Marres and author of Big Data: Does Size Matter Timandra Harkness investigate the dangers and blessings of big data.
subtitle: The stories left behind Big Data

title: Elites in the Dock
description: We see elites as privileged, and undemocratic, and typically up to no good. Yet elites run our schools and our hospitals, our science research labs and our armed forces. Should we stop seeing 'elite' as a term of abuse and require elites to run our politics and media? Or is every elite to be challenged and potentially eradicated? Or are some fields different from others?
speaker_desc: Times columnist and Tony Blair's speechwriter Phillip Collins, activist and engineer Yassmin Abdel-Magied, Cambridge historian of ideas Hugo Drochon and anarchist and former diplomat Carne Ross debate elitism and the elites' roles in society.
subtitle: Are elites necessarily a bad thing?

title: Against Meritocracy
description: Would a meritocratic society ruled by merit provide a fair equality of opportunity? Should we aim to solve social inequality through equality of outcome? NYU philosopher and 2016 Reith Lecturer Kwame Anthony Appiah on inequality in society and confronting the difficult issues of family inheritance
subtitle: Kwame Anthony Appiah | Merit is a mask of class

title: Reason and the Gods
description: Belief in the Gods once filled lives with purpose and a vision of truth. Now many in the secular West dismiss religion yet also rue the loss of meaning and belief. Is this because evidence and reason are not sufficient to make sense of the world?  Is there something about the world that is deeply strange and justifies spirituality?  Or is the worldwide flourishing of religion a temporary blip in human history?
speaker_desc: Sociologist of religion Linda Woodhead, former executive editor of The Economist and author of The Dream of the Enlightenment Anthony Gottlieb, TV presenter and Research Associate at SOAS Centre for Islamic Studies Myriam Francois explore the link between reason and religion.
subtitle: What do secular and religious worldviews share?

title: Post-Truth and Postmodernism
description: Many despise the arrival of a post-truth world and fear politicians who blatantly manipulate facts and peddle falsehoods. But does this rely on assuming that truth is objective and falsehoods can be simply identified? Does the demise of truth mark the end of centuries of progress? Or is truth a construct of the powerful and post-truth a revolution against elites?
subtitle: Is truth just a construct?

title: After Identity Politics
description: Has the left sacrificed solidarity for social conflict? In his book ‘The Once and Future Liberal: After Identity Politics’, Historian of Ideas Mark Lilla argues identity-focused politics has torn the US Trump vs Clinton electorate apart and issues a rallying cry for the left to get together and start winning back power.
subtitle: Mark Lilla | What is the future of the liberal?

title: Everywhere, Somewhere and Nowhere
description: Labour MP Angela Eagle, Demos Director David Goodhart and former Tory MP Anna Soubry debate. Politics was once a question of left and right. Following the Brexit vote, the election of Trump and the rise of populism, is it now a question of nowheres and somewheres? Has open vs closed borders become the central political question?
subtitle: David Goodhart's anywheres vs somewheres

title: There's no such thing as free speech
description: As the war on free speech and censorship on American university campuses continues to rage, where should we turn for answers? Arguing that we need a radical rethink of what universities stand for, eminent literary theorist and author of There’s No Such Thing as Free Speech Stanley Fish puts forward a challenge to liberal and conservative icons alike.
subtitle: There is always a limit to speech

title: Witches, Sluts, Feminists
description: What might contemporary witchcraft tell us about identity, prejudice and power? Kristen Solle, author of Witches, Sluts and Feminists, founding editrix of Slutist.com, lecturer at The New School, and author of the book Witches, Sluts, Feminists: Conjuring The Sex Positivee delves into a world of feminist activism and modern magic.
subtitle: Kristen Sollee | A History of Witch Feminism

title: The myths of meritocracy
description: We think all discrimination can and should be eradicated. Yet we happily reward intelligence, and think it right that the smartest get ahead. Is it fair to assume that intelligence deserves reward and is it right to build a society to favour an educated liberal elite? Empires from Rome to the Mongols were built on other qualities. Should we wise up to our own prejudice?  Or is discrimination based on academic merit vital to society?
speaker_desc: Warwick University professor of sociology Steve Fuller, British Conservative politician and author of War and Gold: A Five-Hundred-Year History of Empires, Adventures and Debt Kwasi Kwarteng, and Professor of the Public Understanding of Philosophy at the University of Sheffield Angie Hobbs explore the good, the bad and the ugly of what we have come to call meritocracy.
subtitle: Should we reward intelligence?

title: Can We Control AI?
description: In world with artificial intelligence, how will we maintain control? Sir Nigel Shadbolt, Open Data Institute co-founder, examines how A.I. looks set to reshape our lives and society.
subtitle: Nigel Shadbolt | The right questions to ask on AI

title: The end of the theory of everything
description: Stephen Hawking once predicted a theory of everything by 2000. However, after decades without one he began to doubt its existence. Have we failed because no one theory can make sense of reality? Must we "employ different theories in different situations" as Hawking now suggested, or is there a final theory just waiting to be discovered? Huw Price, John Ellis and Joanna Kavenna debate.
speaker_desc: Cambridge Professor of Philosophy Huw Price, CERN physicist John Ellis and author Joanna Kavenna investigate one of physics' greatest dilemmas.
subtitle: Can we fully describe reality?

title: The art of activism
description: Must activism be creative to make real impact? Philosopher Patricia MacCormack argues political protest is art and that art should always be activism.
subtitle: Creative protest for impact

title: Our sins and our selves
description: Are we wrong to assume that there is a single self behind our actions?  Are people not good or bad but only individual actions?  Should we accept that we are inconsistent and unpredictable? Or is consistency and integrity the cornerstone of what it is to be human? Is the self just a construction, and does that absolve us of moral responsibility or on the contrary, does this mean we have to be more accountable because it assumes more agency?
speaker_desc: Professor of religion, politics and ethics John Millbank, co-founder of The Philosophers' Magazine Julian Baggini and Professor of the Public Understanding of Philosophy Angie Hobbs explore our multiple selves.
subtitle: How morally consistent and good can we be?

title: The Secret History of Cool
description: From James Dean to Kate Moss, we know cool when we see it. But its history goes back to jazz music and the civil rights movement. Academic Joel Dinerstein reveals the forgotten history of this elusive concept. "Entertaining and insightful" - New York Times
subtitle: Joel Dinerstein | Coolness as racial resistance

title: Back from the End of Time
description: The passing of time is an illusion. Or so claims physics since Einstein. Yet we tend to think we do experience time passing. There has been no explanation for how the future might already be fixed in the way the present or past might be, or how we are in some sense already dead while we feel alive.  Do we need a new account of space-time that aligns physics with our experience? Theoretical physicist and winner of the Spinoza Prize Erik Verlinde, Cambridge philosopher Huw Price and Warwick philosopher of science Alison Fernandes investigate time.
speaker_desc: Theoretical physicist and winner of the Spinoza Prize Erik Verlinde, Cambridge philosopher Huw Price and Warwick philosopher of science Alison Fernandes investigate time.
subtitle: Is the passage of time an illusion?

title: Sex, Lies and Pharmacology
description: From antidepressants to acne treatment, are prescription drugs destroying our sex lives? Radical psychiatrist David Healy exposes the hidden side-effects of psychiatric drugs.
subtitle: David Healy | Psychiatric drugs destroy sex lives

title: How We Came to #MeToo
description: Sexual abuse accusations have a reached a new high. Why now? Leading British sociologist Linda Woodhead investigates.
subtitle: Linda Woodhead | The origins of sexual accusations

title: Mechanisms of the Mind
description: How might artificial intelligence change how we think about memory, learning and language? Cognitive scientist Margaret Boden reveals the latest insights on minds and machines.
subtitle: Margaret Boden | Rethinking memory through AI

title: Narrating the Brain
description: King’s College London New Thinkers: how does evidence from neuroscience alter our account of identity? Philosopher Benjamin Dalton argues for a new narrative of the self
subtitle: Benjamin Dalton | Neuroscience's story of the self

title: Who We Are: Beyond Black and White
description: Ten years ago, the US elected its first black president. Yet race-related hate crime has increased 216% in the last year. Are we wrong to suppose that racial prejudice will be overcome by equal opportunity? Should we dream of a world where race is not a basis for social identity? Or are social groupings inevitable and equality the only possible solution
speaker_desc: Kimberlé Crenshaw, Distinguished Professor of Law at UCLA and Columbia Law School, known for coining the concept of intersectionality, UK Labour MP Diane Abbott, Brookings Institute economist Richard Reeves and UK Conservative MP Kemi Badenoch investigate race.
subtitle: Can we have a world where race does not matter?

title: The Secrets of Consciousness
description: Consciousness is a deep puzzle. There was hope that neuroscience might find some answers. But we still have no explanation for where brain activity ends and experience begins. Is it a mistake to think we can explain consciousness by examining the brain? Should we look elsewhere to our evolutionary roots perhaps? Or might neuroscience pull the cat from the bag after all?
speaker_desc: Psychologist and author of Seeing Myself Susan Blackmore, panpsychist and author of Consciousness and Fundamental Reality Philip Goff, and psychologist Nicholas Humphrey, whose books include The Mind Made Flesh and Soul Dust: The Magic of Consciousness , explore the unknown corners of our minds and lives.
subtitle: Can the brain explain experience?

title: Dreams To Believe In
description: Faced with uncertainty, social division, and an unstable and potentially violent world, many fear a dark future. Might this stem not from accident but from a lack of a positive vision - with belief in progress and understanding undermined?  Can we put current troubles down to a temporary blip? Or do we need a new grand vision to sustain and encourage us, and if so what is it?
speaker_desc: Guy Standing : Professor of Development at SOAS, Standing is the world's leading expert on Universal Basic Income and wrote The Precariat: The New Dangerous Class. Phillip Collins : British journalist, academic, banker and speechwriter, Collins is a columnist for The Times and former Chief Speech Writer to Tony Blair. Diane Abbott : Currently the Shadow Home Secretary, Abbott is one of Labour's most prominent frontbenchers and has been a party member since 1987.
subtitle: Does politics need radical political vision?

title: What's Wrong With the Left?
description: Has the left lost its way? Human rights activist Peter Tatchell argues for a return to human rights and social justice to unite the left and reclaim power.
subtitle: Peter Tatchell | Give up the myths, seek alliances

title: Corporation vs. Nation
description: Tax dodges and abuse of monopoly power has led to an outcry against global corporations. With 70 companies now each bigger than half the world's nations, have we mistakenly assumed that unregulated growth is for the good of all?  Should nations fight back to contain corporate power and impose national interests? And if so how?  Or are corporations the drivers of growth and the route out of poverty for the worlds poorest? The Making of Global Capitalism author Leo Panitch, journalist and economist Anatole Kaletsky, and Treasury Secretary Liz Truss examine a global struggle for power.
speaker_desc: The Making of Global Capitalism author Leo Panitch, journalist and economist Anatole Kaletsky, and Treasury Secretary Liz Truss examine a global struggle for power.
subtitle: Should governments aim to contain corporate power?

title: The secrets of the uncanny
description: We associate the uncanny with fiction and David Lynch movies. Yet most of us have had the feeling of being lost in somewhere known or the eerieness of deja vu. Is the uncanny more than a literary device? Does it uncover the unconscious? Or perhaps point to a genuine strangeness in the world itself?
speaker_desc: Science fiction author Richard Morgan, Coco de Mer founder Sam Roddick, and post-postmodern philosopher Hilary Lawson find the uncanny everywhere.
subtitle: What does our sense of uncanny say about us?

title: Rich and Equal
description: We are used to the idea that wealth has become ever more focused on a tiny group of the super rich. UK figures, however, show income inequality falling for the last fifteen years. Is this an illusion? Should we reduce income inequality and eradicate inherited wealth to create a fairer society, or are these essential drivers of growth that bring prosperity to all?
speaker_desc: Conservative 'rising star' Kwasi Kwarteng, Big Issue founder John Bird and human rights campaigner Peter Tatchell interrogate inequality.
subtitle: Can a society be equal and prosperous?

title: How To Be Idle
description: Founder and editor of the Idler Magazine, Tom Hodgkinson lays his eye on the foibles of modern life, and offers his advice for how to get by more happily
subtitle: Tom Hodgkinson | The case against efficiency

title: The Oldest Profession
description: Should we decriminalise sex work? In the wake of Jeremy Corbyn’s support, Niki Adams from English Collective of Prostitutes, and Liz Hilton from Empower Foundation, outline the future of the oldest profession.
subtitle: Niki Adams | Should we decriminalise sex work?

title: The Illusion of Race
description: Many assume that different races have different genetic characteristics. Yet it has not been possible to identify a set of genes that typify any particular racial group. Is this simply a failure of genetics? Or is race an illusory construct with no basis in nature that we should seek to eradicate?
speaker_desc: Guardian columnist Zoe Williams, author of The R Word Kurt Barling, and Imperial College London geneticist Anne Bowcock interrogate the concept of race
subtitle: Why genetics defies racism

title: Eating to Save the Planet
description: Former UK Green Party leader Natalie Bennett, yogic monk Dada Jyotirupananda and philosopher T!M Freke investigate how we might eat differently. Biologists claim that the predatory character of humans is leading to the sixth mass extinction. With industrial farming driving this disaster, is it time to radically transform how we think about food and nature? Instead of considering what is best for humans, could we see nature as something sacred? Could this revolutionise how we eat? Or are policy, regulation and practical action the only truly viable solutions?
subtitle: Is it time to rethink our relationship with food?

title: Why Does Time Fly?
description: Why does time flow? What is consciousness? Theoretical physicist and author Bernard Carr seeks one answer to two timeless puzzles.
subtitle: Bernard Carr | Time and consciousness

title: Beyond the Standard Model
description: Have we caught sight of the first new particle after the Higgs boson? Cambridge University Research Fellow Tevong You ushers in the next era of the universe.
subtitle: Tevong You | The first new particle after Higgs

title: Can Facebook Save Itself?
description: The internet and computing giants transformed our world with new technologies and potential. Yet tax issues and privacy fears have meant that they are increasingly seen as malevolent monopolies threatening governments and democracy. Is big necessarily bad? And if so how do we protect ourselves? Or should we stop moaning and enjoy the products?
speaker_desc: Shadow Minister for Business Chi Onwurah, journalist and author of Capitalism 4.0 Anatole Kaletsky, and outspoken economic historian Deirdre McCloskey debate the power of the tech giants.
subtitle: Internet giants between the market and regulation

title: A Woman's World
description: What would a feminist utopia like like? Author of Wilful Blindness Margaret Heffernan defies the status quo to imagine real change.
subtitle: Margaret Heffernan | On radical feminist futures

title: Michelangelo vs Damien Hirst
description: Nearly a century ago Duchamp's Fountain placed concept over craft and skill. Yet many still think the classic works of the canon remain unrivalled. Did art lose its way? Does our reverence for the old masters show that art needs more than a clever idea? Or will the test of time count unmade beds and formaldehyde sharks as equal with the Sistine Chapel?
speaker_desc: Young British Artist Gavin Turk, critic and author of Con Art Julian Spalding, and author of Art Wash Mel Evans pit the contemporary against the canon.
subtitle: Has contemporary art lost its way?

title: The Self and the Selfie
description: With more data stored from one day's selfies than all the world's books, many have dismissed Generation Selfie as superficial and vain. Yet creative genius has often been linked to narcissism - Dali once quipped there was no greater joy than waking up as himself. Could focusing on ourselves rather than others be a route to happiness and success? Or is an obsession with ourselves damaging to social cohesion and a likely route to personal misery?
speaker_desc: Philosopher and author of Mirror, mirror: the Uses and Abuses of Self-Love, Simon Blackburn, associate editor of Cosmopolitan magazine Amy Grier, Guardian journalist Tim Dowling, and Instragram influencer Doll Cat Pvssy debate self-obsession on social media.
subtitle: Can focusing on oneself bring about happiness?

title: Global Overhaul
description: Philosopher and Green Party politician Rupert Read explores our moral obligations to the planet.
subtitle: Rupert Read | Why going green matters

title: Decoding the Universe
description: Is information fundamental to the universe? Is reality no more than a strange string of code? Oxford University constructor theorist Chiara Marletto outlines a new theory which seeks to explain life, the universe and everything in it.
subtitle: Chiara Marletto | Reality as a string of code

title: Securing Our Future
description: From LHC black holes to wars against robots, humanity faces new risks that are improbable but catastrophic. Oxford futurist Anders Sandberg outlines how we can save ourselves.
subtitle: Anders Sandberg | How to avoid global disasters

title: Seeing Through Psychosis
description: What can we learn from the experiences of psychosis? Actor and Comedian Juliette Burton uses her experience of mental illness to explore the strange world we're in.
subtitle: Juliette Burton | Illuminated by mental illness

title: The future of the post-truth world
description: Many are fearful as we rush headlong into a post-truth world. Post-truth may have begun as an attack on the lies and deceit of politicians, but it has now become the description of our age. The digital revolution was supposed to herald a new era of openness. Instead it has uncovered a myriad of contradictory perspectives and untrustworthy 'truths' where the loudest and most powerful threaten to be the only winners. So what is the truth about the world? Do we have to accept that, along with the liberal consensus, the era of objective truth is over? Or is there a way to row back from the chaos? And if post-truth is unavoidable, how should we make sense of the world, and more importantly, how might we make it a better place?
speaker_desc: Cambridge University professor of philosophy Rae Langton, Closure theorist Hilary Lawson and author of Post-Truth: Knowledge as a Power Game Steve Fuller dissect the future of the post-truth world. Journalist Polly Toynbee hosts.
subtitle: Is the era of objective truth over?

title: Return to Radical Feminism
description: Has contemporary feminism lost its way? London Feminist Network founder Finn Mackay brings 70s radicalism into the 21st century.
subtitle: Finn Mackay | Has current feminism lost its way?

title: Duchamp's Deception
description: Duchamp’s infamous urinal gave birth to modern art as we know it. But was its founding father a fraud? Outspoken author and critic Julian Spalding uncovers a scandal.
subtitle: Julian Spalding | Was Duchamp a fraud?

title: Doctors in the Age of Google
description: Most of us still think doctor knows best. Yet a third of all hospital beds are filled with conditions caused by medical intervention. With sophisticated diagnosis just a web search away is it time to rid ourselves of medical authority? Or do we need doctors more than ever in the chaos of information?
speaker_desc: Psychiatrist Dr. David Nutt, director of ResPublica, Phillip Blond, and radical GP David Healy envisage the future of medical authority. Mary Ann Sieghart hosts.
subtitle: Is it time to rid ourselves of medical authority?

title: Corruption and Climate Change
description: Is science more sinister than an honest pursuit of the truth? Outspoken astrophysicist Piers Corbyn reveals the hidden power structures that threaten our future in our free online video debate.
subtitle: Piers Corbyn | We misunderstood climate change

title: Dangerous Convictions
description: Nietzsche warned certainty leads to madness. Yet we still demand it of ourselves and others. Sociologist and author of Culture of Fear Frank Furedi asks: could we live without it?
subtitle: Frank Furedi | Could we live without certainty?

title: Democracy and the Digital Revolution
description: Why have we let the internet disrupt the human experience? Corbyn's Shadow Minister for digital government and cyber security Chi Onwurah calls for a democratic revolution.
subtitle: Chi Onwurah | How can technology help democracy?

title: The Emperor's New Art
description: From the masks and jewellery of the Pharaohs to contemporary painting, art has always been valued above almost all else. Yet it has no practical purpose. Has money chased art because, with no objective measure, art is victim to limitless hype and fashion, or are gold baubles and diamond skulls of genuinely great value?
speaker_desc: Design guru and author of Ugly Stephen Bayley, philosopher Andrew Bowie, and activist and author of Art Wash Mel Evans ask how art gets its pricetag.
subtitle: From where does art get its value?

title: Life in the Universe
description: What does the hunt for extra-terrestrial life say about human nature? What will happen if the radio silence stops? Theologian, astrophysicist and author of God, Time & Stephen Hawking David Wilkinson explores.
subtitle: David Wilkinson | Why we search for life in space

title: What should we do about poverty?
description: Is government policy exacerbating poverty? Big Issue founder John Bird takes the government to task as he discusses his new political manifesto. "Eccentric, extraordinary but worldly wise" Polly Toynbee
subtitle: Big Issue Founder John Bird's Political Manifesto

title: In Search of Safety
description: Visions of a violent and lawless future are a commonplace, yet strangely crime has fallen 66% in the UK in the last two decades and we are less likely to fall victim to an act of violence than we have ever been. Do we want to imagine the world is dangerous because our lives have become too safe? Or is the world scarier than the figures suggest?
speaker_desc: Former Anglican Priest Chris Bryant, feminist Finn Mackay and outspoken libertarian and editor of Spiked Online Brendan O'Neill examine risk.
subtitle: Is the world as dangerous as it seems?

title: Democracy and Drugs
description: David Nutt was fired by the Home Secretary for comparing the harms of ecstasy and horse-riding. Hear his case for an evidence-based approach to drug policy and resurrecting the use of psychedelics as a treatment for mental illness.
subtitle: Using psychedelics to treat mental illness

title: The Death Drive
description: car crash; celebrity; celebrity culture; car; top gear; the grand tour; famous car crashes; car accident; car crash as cultural phenomenon; analysis of car crashes; car crash statistics;
subtitle: The car crash as a 20th century phenomenon

title: In the Beginning Was the Word
description: In the 20th century we came to see language as radically more important than a mere vehicle for ideas. It was the framework that made thought possible.  But do animals not think? And can't humans think outside of language - knowing the way home for example? Is language not so central after all or is there really nothing outside of the text?
speaker_desc: New York philosopher and author of Descriptions Stephen Neale, Closure theorist Hilary Lawson, and existential novelist Janne Teller look beyond words.
subtitle: Is the  world dependent on language?

title: The New Bodies
description: Society now accepts gender and sexuality as fluid. Is the fluidity of the human body the next step forward? Bionic hand user and transhumanist Nicky Ashwell envisions the future.
subtitle: Transhumanism: Rise of the Cyborgs

title: Love Is the Drug
description: We’re happy taking drugs to fight depression. But what about a pill for engineering romance? Oxford neuroscientist and Future of Humanity Institute fellow Anders Sandberg makes the case for chemically enhancing our love lives.
speaker_desc: Oxford neuroscientist and Future of Humanity Institute fellow Anders Sandberg makes the case for chemically enhancing our love lives.
subtitle: Can we have a pill that sparks love?

title: Culture Shock
description: We think culture is always evolving. Yet from the death of subculture to our obsession with everything old-school, we seem in a strange cultural lull. Where are our punks, our Picassos and our Freuds? Has our culture run out of ideas, or are the great ideas and movements for our time already with us or just round the corner?

subtitle: Have we run out of radical ideas?

So where is the limit between what computers, or robots, can and cannot actually do? When might machines match their makers? Or is this idea just a hype caused by a misunderstanding of what artificial intelligence is?
speaker_desc: Philosophers David Chalmers and Kate Devlin join Closure theorist Hilary Lawson to consider the threat of intelligent machines.

Kate Soper debate our place in the world.
